reason: The forward implication follows by testing all exponents annihilating \(-a\). The converse is repaired by using that \((p-1)/2\) is odd; the supplied proof instead mistakenly wrote a congruence modulo \(2\) and incorrectly invoked order \(p-1\) for \(-a\).
text:
Let \(m=(p-1)/2=2t+1\), which is odd.

First suppose that \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\), so \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1=2m\). Then \(a^m\not\equiv1\pmod p\), while \((a^m)^2\equiv1\pmod p\). Since \(p\) is odd, this implies \(a^m\equiv-1\pmod p\). Hence
\[
(-a)^m=(-1)^m a^m\equiv(-1)(-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
If \((-a)^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then \(a^{2n}=(-a)^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\). Since \(a\) has order \(2m\), we have \(2m\mid2n\), and therefore \(m\mid n\). Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m=(p-1)/2\).

Conversely, suppose that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m\). Put \(x=-a\), so \(x\) has the odd order \(m\) and \(a=-x\). Certainly
\[
a^{2m}=(-x)^{2m}=x^{2m}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Now suppose that \(a^n=(-x)^n\equiv1\pmod p\). If \(n\) were odd, then \(x^n\equiv-1\pmod p\). Squaring would give \(x^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\), so \(m\mid2n\). Because \(m\) is odd, \(m\mid n\), which would imply \(x^n\equiv1\pmod p\), a contradiction since \(p\) is odd. Therefore \(n\) is even. Then \(x^n=a^n\equiv1\pmod p\), so \(m\mid n\). Since \(m\) is odd and \(n\) is even, \(2m\mid n\). Consequently \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=2m=p-1\), and hence \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).
